questions.stem: A 60-kg patient receives 600 mg of a drug as an IV bolus. The extrapolated plasma concentration at time zero is 20 mg/L. Where is this drug most likely distributed?

options.D: Concentrated in tissues far beyond body water
options.E: Bound almost entirely to plasma albumin

questions.explanation: Vd = 600 mg / 20 mg/L = 30 L = 0.5 L/kg, close to total body water (~0.55 L/kg). A: Plasma is ~0.05 L/kg. B: ECF is ~0.2 L/kg. D: Tissue concentration gives Vd > ~1 L/kg. E: Extensive albumin binding keeps Vd near plasma volume.

questions.stem: A patient stable on phenytoin (a weak acid, highly bound to albumin) develops severe hepatic disease with low serum albumin. The total phenytoin level is unchanged. What is the main risk?

options.B: Toxicity from an increased free fraction
options.E: No change, because total levels are normal

questions.explanation: Low albumin → fewer binding sites → more free (active) drug even at the same total level. A: Binding falls, not rises. C: Protein binding doesn't govern GI absorption. D: More free drug means more is available to cross into tissues. E: The total level hides the rise in free drug.

questions.stem: A patient on propranolol, a weak base, is admitted with an acute severe illness. How is the free (unbound) fraction of propranolol most likely to change?

options.B: Increase, because α1-acid glycoprotein synthesis falls
options.D: Decrease, because α1-acid glycoprotein synthesis rises
options.E: No change, because weak bases don't bind plasma proteins

questions.explanation: Weak bases bind mainly the positively charged α1-acid glycoprotein, whose synthesis increases during an acute insult → more binding, lower free fraction. A: Albumin falls in acute illness but binds mainly weak acids (phenytoin, salicylates). B: α1-acid glycoprotein rises, not falls. C: Albumin falls, and it isn't propranolol's main carrier. E: Weak bases bind α1-acid glycoprotein (e.g., quinidine, propranolol).

questions.stem: Domperidone, a dopamine antagonist that doesn't cross the blood–brain barrier, still relieves nausea through a central site. What best explains this?

options.A: It is highly lipid-soluble and diffuses through the tight junctions
options.B: The chemoreceptor trigger zone lies where the barrier is leaky
options.C: P-glycoprotein pumps it into the brain
options.D: Brain endothelial MAO and COMT convert it to an active metabolite
options.E: Nausea makes the barrier leaky everywhere

questions.explanation: The BBB is leaky at the chemoreceptor trigger zone, so domperidone (and apomorphine) can act there without entering the rest of the brain. A: If it diffused freely it would cross the BBB everywhere. C: P-gp is an efflux pump that keeps drugs out of the brain. D: Endothelial MAO and COMT neutralize drugs; they are part of the barrier. E: Infection, not nausea, is the pathological factor that makes the barrier leakier.

questions.stem: A pregnant woman takes a weakly basic drug. At equilibrium, the fetal plasma concentration of the drug is higher than the maternal concentration. What best explains this?

options.A: Fetal plasma is more alkaline, trapping the ionized base
options.B: P-glycoprotein actively pumps the drug into the fetus
options.C: The placenta is completely impermeable to acids
options.D: Fetal plasma is slightly more acidic, trapping the ionized base
options.E: Fetal albumin binds bases more strongly

questions.explanation: In the slightly more acidic fetal plasma, a base becomes more ionized and can't diffuse back (ion trapping). A: Alkaline plasma would keep a base unionized. B: P-gp exports drugs and limits fetal exposure. C: The placenta isn't an absolute barrier. E: Albumin binds mainly acids.

questions.stem: After an overdose of imipramine (Vd > 10 L/kg), hemodialysis removes very little drug. What best explains this?

options.A: Imipramine is confined to plasma, bound to albumin
options.B: Imipramine distributes only in total body water
options.C: Most of the drug is concentrated in tissues, so little is in plasma
options.D: A large Vd means the drug is eliminated too quickly to need dialysis
options.E: Imipramine is a large protein that can't cross dialysis membranes

questions.explanation: A Vd far above total body water (> 1 L/kg) means the drug is concentrated in tissues; only a small fraction is in plasma, where dialysis acts. A: Plasma-confined drugs (heparin, insulin) have Vd ~0.05–0.1 L/kg. B: Total body water corresponds to ~0.55 L/kg (e.g., ethanol). D: Vd describes distribution, not speed of elimination. E: Imipramine is a small lipophilic drug, not a protein.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man with decompensated heart failure and marked peripheral edema receives a standard weight-based IV dose of gentamicin, a water-soluble antibiotic. His peak plasma level is lower than expected. Why?

options.C: Increased P-glycoprotein efflux in the gut
options.D: Faster renal clearance from heart failure
options.E: Increased Vd from expanded extracellular water

questions.explanation: Edema expands extracellular water, so a water-soluble drug spreads into a larger apparent Vd → lower peak concentration. A: Gentamicin has low protein binding, and less binding wouldn't lower the peak. B: There is no first pass after IV dosing. C: Gut P-gp is irrelevant to an IV drug. D: Heart failure tends to reduce renal clearance.

questions.stem: A pilot with allergic rhinitis is switched from diphenhydramine to loratadine and no longer feels drowsy. Which property of loratadine best explains this?

options.A: It doesn't cross the blood–brain barrier well
options.B: It is a competitive H2 antagonist
options.C: It has much lower plasma protein binding
options.D: It is excreted unchanged by the kidney
options.E: It has a very small volume of distribution

questions.explanation: Second-generation H1 antihistamines are less lipophilic and are P-gp substrates, so little reaches the CNS; first-generation agents are lipophilic and cross the BBB. B: Loratadine is an H1 antagonist. C: Lower binding would increase free drug and wouldn't explain less sedation. D: The route of excretion doesn't determine CNS entry. E: A small Vd isn't the reason it spares the brain.

questions.stem: In Parkinson disease, the brain needs more dopamine, yet patients are given levodopa (L-DOPA) rather than dopamine. Why?

options.A: Dopamine is too lipid-soluble and stays in body fat
options.B: L-DOPA is small enough to diffuse through the BBB tight junctions
options.C: L-DOPA enters the brain via LAT1, then becomes dopamine
options.D: The BBB is leaky in Parkinson disease, but only for L-DOPA
options.E: Dopamine crosses the BBB but is pumped back out by P-glycoprotein

questions.explanation: Dopamine can't cross the BBB; L-DOPA is carried across by the LAT1 transporter and then converted to dopamine inside the brain. A: Dopamine is blocked by the BBB, not trapped in fat. B: L-DOPA needs a transporter; it isn't simple diffusion. D: Infection, not Parkinson disease, is the lecture's example of a leakier barrier. E: Dopamine is simply blocked; the lecture lists it among substances that don't cross.
